A false negative exposes the cost; if two photographs of the same dog appear as alternatives, the loss pushes apart items that the intended task may want together. Better data, multiple positive views, or rules that avoid likely duplicates can reduce the damage, but none removes the need to state what relation matters. Contrastive learning gives a flexible way to learn that relation; it does not settle the philosophical question of what meaning is.

The sequence in this chapter is now clear. Counting gathered the company of symbols and compressed it. Prediction learned to anticipate a neighbour as data arrived. Contrast kept the useful comparison but replaced a complete vocabulary with a local contest, and with it the limit that a vocabulary set. Any two views that can be paired can be embedded together, so the same recipe reaches images, sounds and text, and the tools stay Shannon's, since the loss is a cross-entropy and its value bounds, in bits, the mutual information between the two views. That made embeddings practical for rich signals and opened a path toward shared spaces, yet it still relies on alternatives to keep the space from collapsing into one point. The next section asks whether a model can keep only what is predictable and important without a vocabulary or negatives at all. Its answer introduces a new danger. If every input becomes the same vector, prediction is perfect and the representation says nothing.

::: {.questions}
1. The neighbour to predict is now an image of 8×8 pixels with 16 grey levels each. How many terms would the denominator of the softmax of Learning by Prediction have? How many terms does the InfoNCE loss have with a batch of 256 pairs? Why does this pseudo-normalization work? Hint: the negatives are drawn with the frequency of the data.

2. Two photographs of the same cat differ in the lighting and in the noise of the sensor. A model predicts the second photograph from the first with a squared error; another is trained contrastively, with photographs of other cats as negatives. Which of the two is charged for the lighting, and which for the noise of the sensor?

3. Using `numpy` (or a library with automatic differentiation) and the 8×8 digits of scikit-learn (`load_digits`, scaled to $[0,1]$), train an encoder with InfoNCE and no labels. A positive pair is two augmented views of the same image, each shifted by $-1$, $0$ or $1$ pixel in each direction and with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.15; the negatives of an image are the other images of its batch. The encoder maps the 64 pixels to 128 hidden units with ReLU and then to 16 coordinates, which are normalized to unit norm, and the scores are the dot products divided by $\tau = 0.2$. Train on 1,200 images and keep 597 for testing, with 2,000 steps of Adam (learning rate $10^{-3}$), for the batch sizes $N = 2, 8, 32, 128$ and five seeds each. Hint: the gradient of the loss with respect to the scores is the softmax minus the identity, divided by $N$, as in the box of Learning by Prediction. As a contrast, train the same encoder, with a linear read-out of the 16 coordinates to 64 pixels, to predict the pixels of the other view with a squared error. For each method, and for raw pixels and a PCA with 16 dimensions, report the retrieval (the fraction of test images for which, among 597 augmented test views, the view most similar by cosine to a view of the image is another view of the same image, after subtracting the mean of the views), and for InfoNCE the loss and the bound $\log_2 N - \ell_N$ in bits. Then compute the alignment (mean squared distance between the unit vectors of the two views of an image), the uniformity ($\log$ of the mean of $e^{-2d^2}$ over pairs of different images) and the offset (the length of the mean of the vectors divided by their mean length), and draw the histograms of the cosines of views of the same image and of different images. Why is the bound below $\log_2 N$, what does it tell us that it still rises with $N$, and what do the histograms say about what each method keeps?
:::

::: {.answers}
1. The softmax sums over every possible neighbour, here $16^{64} = 2^{256} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{77}$ images, so it cannot even be written down. InfoNCE sums over 256 candidates: the positive and the 255 other members of the batch. The batch sum works as a normalization because the negatives are drawn with the frequency $p(y)$ of the data. The full normalizer is an average over $y \sim p$, $Z(x) = \sum_y p(y)\,e^{s(x,y)}$, and the 255 negatives are a sample of it, an unbiased estimate of $Z(x)$ to which the positive adds one term.

2. The squared error charges every detail of the second photograph that the first one lets the model predict, the lighting among them. The noise of the sensor is independent between the photographs, so it cannot be predicted and only sets a floor on the error. The contrastive model is charged only for what separates this cat from the other photographs of the batch, which includes neither the noise nor the lighting, unless the lighting happens to tell the cat apart from the negatives.

3. The script `contrast_digits_infonce.py` does it (about ten seconds) and saves @fig-contrast-bound and @fig-contrast-cosines in `figures/embedding_spaces`. The results are in @tbl-contrast-digits (the script also prints the minimum and maximum over the seeds of every column, and the 5-nearest-neighbour accuracy of the raw pixels, 98.3%, which is why label accuracy would hide the effect).

    With $N = 2$ the encoder is worse than the raw pixels, from $N = 8$ it is better, and with $N = 128$ it finds the other view 3.5 times as often as the pixels do. The bound is below $\log_2 N$ because the loss cannot be negative, and here it stays far below (4.0 against 7 bits at $N = 128$), because the two views of an image differ by a shift and noise, so the encoder cannot always tell the positive from the other candidates and the loss does not reach zero. It still rises with $N$, so the smaller batches under-estimate the information between the two views, and 4.0 bits is a lower bound, not its value; we do not see where it would stop. The bound is computed from the training loss, but on batches of held-out images it differs by at most 0.05 bits, so it is not an artefact of memorizing the 1,200 images. The table does not separate the effect of the batch from that of the training, since a different encoder is trained for each $N$.

    The histograms show what each method keeps. The cosines of the raw pixels are never negative, because pixels are, and views of the same image are hardly separated from different images (a). The predictor puts everything in a narrow cone; the mean of its vectors is 96% as long as the vectors themselves (for InfoNCE with $N = 128$ it is 10%, and for $N = 2$ 46%), a shared offset that gives it the best alignment and the worst uniformity (b); it spends its 16 coordinates on reproducing the pixels, the brightness included, and after the mean is subtracted it retrieves about as well as the raw pixels (13.9% against 11.1%, and one seed is at 11.7%). InfoNCE with $N = 2$ only has to beat one other image, a coarse feature is enough, and the two histograms overlap (c); with $N = 128$ the different images are spread around cosine 0 and the views of the same image stay mostly above 0.7 (d). The vectors also spread out as $N$ grows, as the alignment and uniformity picture above suggests; the uniformity falls from $-2.10$ at $N = 2$ to $-3.07$ at $N = 128$, and the alignment from 0.51 to 0.28. This is consistent with the contrastive vector keeping what tells one image from the others and not what is needed to rebuild it, but one encoder and one read-out do not prove it; the predictor could do better with another architecture or another bottleneck.
:::

## Learning by Predicting Embeddings {.provisional}

*Plan (2–3 pages).* A fourth objective, which keeps prediction but changes its target. Learning by Prediction predicts the neighbour itself, and pays in bits for every detail of it; Learning by Contrast picks the neighbour out of a batch of negatives. A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) predicts the *embedding* of a missing part from the embedding of its context: two encoders, one for the context and one for the target, and a predictor between them, with the loss measured as a distance in the embedding space rather than as a surprisal over the vocabulary. What cannot be predicted from the context need not be represented, so the vector keeps what is predictable from the context, with no softmax over a vocabulary and no negatives. data2vec (2022) applies the idea to text, speech, and images alike, predicting at masked positions the averaged inner-layer vectors of a target network [@baevski2022data2vec]; the image and video forms named JEPA are told in @sec-ch-multimodal-embeddings.

The price of dropping negatives is collapse. If every input is mapped to the same vector, the prediction is perfect and the space says nothing; a milder failure, dimensional collapse, uses only a few of the $d$ directions. Negatives were what kept the space spread out, Wang and Isola's uniformity [@wang2020understanding], so something else must do it. Two answers, told as history: an asymmetric design in which the target encoder is a slowly moving average of the context encoder (BYOL, 2020) [@grill2020bootstrap], and explicit terms that keep the variance of every coordinate up and their covariances down (VICReg, 2022) [@bardes2022vicreg]. Both were designed for two augmented views of one input, not for a context and a masked part, but they solve the same problem of avoiding collapse without negatives. VICReg's explicit terms do by hand what uniformity did through negatives.

- Claim: the four objectives differ in what the vector pays for. Counting pays in reconstruction error on the whole PMI matrix, prediction in bits for every detail of the neighbour. Contrast pays only for what separates the positive from the negatives, and latent prediction only for what is predictable from the context. The last two differ in what keeps the space from collapsing: negatives in one, a moving-average target or a variance term in the other.
- Cost and scale: latent prediction is argued for as the general method for signals too rich to predict in detail [@lecun2022path], and against it as a prior that scaled generative models absorb; the question is left to the closing section of @sec-ch-generative-spaces, where both are on the table.
- Hooks: collapse as the extreme of the anisotropy of Where a Single Vector Strains and of the directions of @sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality; prediction in latent space and world models in @sec-ch-multimodal-embeddings; predictive processing in the Epilogue.
- Exercise: train a toy latent predictor on the corpus of this chapter, watch it collapse, measure the effective rank of the embeddings, and restore it with a moving-average target or a variance term.

## Learning by Reconstruction {.idea}

*Plan (2–3 pages).* The objectives so far guess a neighbour, pick it out among candidates, or guess its code. Reconstruction goes back to guessing the data, but the input itself and through a small code, so the vector must keep whatever the rebuilding needs; it is the `predict the other view` model of Learning by Contrast with the data as the only target. The linear case is the truncated SVD of From Counting to Geometry: the best rank-$d$ approximation of a matrix (Eckart and Young) is a linear encoder and decoder, $\mathbf{M}\approx\mathbf{E}\mathbf{V}^\top$ [@eckart1936approximation], and the "latent" of latent semantic analysis is this case. A nonlinear autoencoder generalizes it; a denoising autoencoder reconstructs the clean input from a corrupted one, which is the first step towards @sec-ch-generative-spaces. What the code keeps (what is needed to rebuild, brightness included) against what a contrastive code keeps (what separates). Is an autoencoder a generative model? Its decoder does generate a point from a code, but nothing says which codes are valid, so it defines no distribution to sample from or to score; adding a prior makes it one (the variational autoencoder, in the next chapter). No guarantee that distance in the code means anything. Exercise: a linear autoencoder against the SVD (same subspace), then a nonlinear one on the digits of the contrast experiment (script `reconstruct_digits_ae.py`, reusing its data, split and measures).
- Claim: of the five objectives it is the one that pays for every detail of the input, in error measured in the data, and the only one with a way back from the vector to the data; that way back is what the next chapter builds on.

## The Geometry of Meaning {.provisional}

*Plan (3–4 pages).* On the unit sphere cosine similarity and Euclidean distance carry the same information, $\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_2^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta$; the direction of a vector encodes its category and its norm encodes frequency and salience. Mikolov's analogy parallelogram, $\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}$ [@mikolov2013efficient], and why it follows from ratios of co-occurrence probabilities becoming differences of logarithms [@arora2016latent; @pennington2014glove]. This is where GloVe belongs: it fits the vectors by a weighted least squares on the logarithms of the non-zero counts, $\sum f(C_{wc})(\langle \mathbf{e}_w, \mathbf{v}_c\rangle + b_w + \tilde b_c - \ln C_{wc})^2$, so the dot product is again a PMI, and its derivation starts from those ratios. A brief note on steering vectors: the same linear structure, found inside the activations of LLMs of the 2020s, and developed in @sec-ch-contextual-vectors as the linear representation hypothesis. Keep three claims apart: that dot products are what hardware computes cheaply (why linear read-outs scale), that concepts are directions in learned spaces (an empirical claim about what training finds), and that general methods beat built-in knowledge (a claim about methods, which does not say that the winner is linear). Exercise: test analogies on pre-trained vectors and find where they fail.

## Where a Single Vector Strains {.provisional}

*Plan (2–3 pages).* Anisotropy: embeddings trained by some objectives crowd into a narrow cone, so that all cosines are high, and the simple remedies of centring and whitening. Contrastive objectives with many negatives often exert the opposite pressure, spreading vectors across available directions. Hubness, a few points that are the nearest neighbour of almost everything, a high-dimensional effect from @sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality, now seen in a trained space. Close with, in prose, the ledger of limits that the rest of the book examines. Each is stated as a cost, not as an impossibility, and each says whether it is structural or contingent: whatever the objective, a map from data to vectors says nothing about how likely a point is or what lies between the data, and a model that does say it has distances that mean only what its training made them mean (@sec-ch-generative-spaces); a model that can sample produces what is plausible without checking it, which retrieval addresses in part (@sec-ch-vector-databases); one vector per word cannot follow the sentence the word appears in, so the vector must become contextual, and a contextual vector must then hold more features than it has dimensions (@sec-ch-contextual-vectors); a nearest-neighbour query cannot negate or chain, and a fixed-dimension dot product can realize only a limited family of rankings (@sec-ch-vector-databases); flat space needs more dimensions than curved space to hold a hierarchy at the same distortion (@sec-ch-tangent-spaces-geodesics); symmetric dot products cannot express asymmetric relations (@sec-ch-graph-embeddings); pairwise structure does not directly encode multi-way interactions (@sec-ch-topological-deep-learning); similarity alone is not a logic, because negation and conjunction need more than a score (@sec-ch-complex-plane-quantum-logic); a sum of vectors cannot say which attribute belongs to which object, the binding problem (@sec-ch-vector-symbolic-architectures); systematic composition is the open question of @sec-ch-neurosymbolic-integration; the coordinates of a trained space are arbitrary up to an isometry, so comparing two spaces is a problem of its own (@sec-ch-cross-domain-transfer); a space shared across senses keeps only what its views have in common, while embeddings of different modalities remain in separate cones, the modality gap (@sec-ch-multimodal-embeddings); and a book, or a subject at several levels of detail, held as one vector keeps neither its parts nor the zoom, and similarity alone cannot check that the parts agree with each other or with verified sources (multiple vectors per item in @sec-ch-vector-databases, trees in @sec-ch-tangent-spaces-geodesics, the order of prerequisites in @sec-ch-graph-embeddings, capacity in @sec-ch-vector-symbolic-architectures, consistency in @sec-ch-complex-plane-quantum-logic and @sec-ch-neurosymbolic-integration), which is the critical literacy test of the Prologue. End on the other side of the ledger: the thesis is not that a single vector fails and a richer geometry repairs it, but that a single vector is a strong first answer and every extension is a trade. For each limit the question is whether more dimensions, data and compute substitute for the added structure.

## A Space That Cannot Yet Say No {.provisional}

*Plan (1 page).* Findings: counting, predicting, contrasting, predicting embeddings and reconstructing are different routes to the same kind of object, a map whose distances come from Shannon's own quantities, and they differ in what the vector pays for. Achieved for the representation of meaning: nearness is likeness, difference is a relation and a direction is a meaning one can move along, now as measurements from a corpus and no longer as promises. Computation: prediction bought an algorithm that uses computation well (memory proportional to the vocabulary, a cost per step independent of the corpus, steps that run in parallel, vectors that keep improving with more text); whether latent prediction is the general method, or a prior that scaled generative models absorb, is left to the generative chapter. Still out of reach: a map from data to vectors cannot say how likely a point is, cannot negate, and cannot keep a book, a hierarchy or a binding intact; each is an entry of the ledger, and the chapter that takes it up is named there. The first is answered by a sampler (@sec-ch-generative-spaces) and the last, the limit that a nearest-neighbour query cannot say no, is tested in @sec-ch-complex-plane-quantum-logic.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Further Reading {.unnumbered}

Counting, predicting and contrasting are not unrelated techniques but convergent estimators of the same co-occurrence statistics. @arora2016latent develops the latent-variable argument for why PMI-based factorization and log-bilinear regression agree, and @pennington2014glove derives the GloVe objective in full. The Prologue states the pattern that this chapter traces from counting to predicting to contrasting. For the PCA and SVD material of "From Counting to Geometry", @hastie2009elements (Section 14.5) is a standard textbook treatment, and @eckart1936approximation is the original proof that truncating the SVD gives the best low-rank approximation. The next chapter's argument about embedding dimensionality rests on the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma [@johnson1984extensions, pp. 189-206], which bounds how much a point set can be projected into lower dimensions while approximately preserving pairwise distances.
